Reproductive Outcomes

Every spring from 1989 to 2025, we trapped female squirrels repeatedly during pregnancy to palpate them and track their pregnancies up to and following gestation. When pregnant females were estimated to be within five days of their parturition date, we fitted them with a very high frequency (VHF) radio collar. Once post-partum (parturition identified by large body mass loss or expressing milk from nipples), using the VHF collar, we tracked the female to her nest. We extracted the pups from the nest to determine litter size, and individual sex and weight. We weighed individual pups to the nearest 0.1 g and gave them a unique ear notch to later identify them within the litter and collect a tissue sample for subsequent DNA parentage analyses (REF). Approximately 25 days after the first visit, we re-located the nest and retrieved the pups. Now developed enough, we ear tagged the pups with unique identification codes and weighed them again to the nearest 0.1 g. To calculate juvenile growth rate, we subtracted the weight at the first visit from the weight at the second weight and divided the difference by the number of days in between visits. Juvenile growth during this time period is linear (REF McAdam & Boutin, 2003 J Evol Biol). SOme litters did not survive to the second nest entry, so we could not obtain growth rates for all litters. For this analysis we only used data from a mother’s first litter on a given year to be consistent with previous studies (REF). We removed cases where the number of days in between weight measurements was less than 5, the first weight was greater than 50 g, or the second weight was greater than 100 g because these are characteristics of instances when a nest was initially sampled too late after parturition to be compared. We then averaged the growth rates for each litter so that each female had only one litter averaged growth rate per year.

We had a total sample size of `r dat[, .N]` litters from `r length(unique(dat$mother_id))` mothers collected from squirrels on two adjacent study areas from 1989-2025. We also collected the parturition dates of all litters because litters born later in the year are usually smaller in size and growth rate (REF). If a litter's parturition date was unknown (n = `r dat[part_source == "estimated", .N]`), e.g., the first nest visit occurred later than normal, we estimated it by subtracting the number of days from the first nest visit to when the pup size would have been the average birth weight of 8 g via the average growth rate of 1.8 g per day (i.e., birth date = date 1 - (weight 1 - 8)/1.8) (REF). Mother age and birth year can also influence life history outcomes (REF). Therefore, we also collected the mothers' birth years from the study's birth record data. If a mother's birth year was unknown (n = `r dat[mombirth_source == "trapping", .N]`), i.e., we do not have a birth record of the mother, we assumed it to be the year before she was first entered into the study. The final life history measurements were litter size, litter growth rate, litter sex ratio (proportion being male), litter parturition date (Julian Day), mother age (years), and mother birth year.


Food Add Experiment

Food supplementation started in `r food[food == 1, min(year)]` and continued until `r food[food == 1, max(year)]`, occurring on `r food[food == 1, length(unique(grid))]` grids (`r food[food == 1, unique(grid)]`). Within the food add grids, buckets of peanut butter were distributed to some middens randomly. These buckets were frequently restocked with peanut butter, to make the food add as close to ad libitum as possible. Natural defensive behaviour by squirrels ensured that buckets were only accessed by the owners of the midden. In total, `r food[food == 1, length(unique(mother_id))]` mothers and `r food[food == 1, .N]` litters were from food add grids, with `r food[treatment_ind == "Bucket", length(unique(mother_id))]` mothers and `r food[treatment_ind == "Bucket", .N]` litters being from middens with buckets. The remainder were from food add grids but did not receive direct food supplementation.


Food Availability Estimates

Natural variation in food availability was measured three different ways, the cone production during the previous year, the mast year status of the current year, and the mother' cache size from the previous year. To assess annual cone production, we counted the number of new cones on 100 trees (average) stratified within each of the `r cones[, length(unique(grid))]` study grids every August from 1988 to 2026. We log transformed the tree cone counts, and took the average for every grid every year. If a grid was not assessed on a given year, we gave it the average tree cone count of all grids measured that year (n = `r dat[cones_prev_source == "average", .N]` litters). Based on cone count data, we categorized years as having normal amounts of cone production or as being mast years, when there were an exponentially high amount of cones produced that autumn (stat?). Over the course of this long term study, `r mast_years` were the mast years. To assess squirrel cache sizes, we counted the number of cones cached on all primary middens in control grids each September starting in 2007 (probably needs more detail).  We log transformed the cached cone counts and paired them to litters born the year following a mother's midden cone count. In total, `r cache[, .N]` litters had associated cache sizes.


Rattle Playback Experiment

In order to test if higher densities affected squirrels non-directly, we experimentally manipulate squirrel perception of density by playing recordings of squirrel rattles to a subset of squirrels. The playback experiments were conducted from 2018 to 2022 on one grid, in addition to a pilot study in 2010 that occurred on three grids. On each grid, speakers were deployed at an average density of XX per ha and were programmed to play squirrel rattles every XX minutes. (I can't speak to much to the actual methods here obviously). In total, `r rattle[food == 19, length(unique(mother_id))]` mothers and `r rattle[food == 19, .N]` litters were from rattle playback grids, while `r rattle[food == 0, length(unique(mother_id))]` mothers and `r rattle[food == 0, .N]` litters were from control grids during those same years.


Local Density

To estimate local densities (squirrels/ha) experienced by mothers in spring, we used the long term census data from the Kluane Red Squirrel Project. Trapping grids were censused every spring in May to determine midden locations and ownership. A squirrel was considered the owner of a midden if it was regularly trapped there and displayed territorial behaviours while on the midden (e.g., rattles). We collected all known squirrels and their midden locations (x, y coordinates) from all years of the spring census data. Occasionally, squirrels may own multiple middens; in these scenarios, we only used the squirrel's primary midden. In total, there were `r census[, .N]` census records of `r census[, length(unique(squirrel_id))]` known squirrels, across the `r census[, length(unique(grid))]` grids and over the `r census[, max(year) - min(year)]` year study. There were `r census[loc_source == "trapping", .N]` census records that had a known squirrel but were missing a location. In these cases, we used the average trapping location of that squirrel that spring (April - June) as their census location.

To calculate local density for each mother, we counted how squirrels resided within a `r radius` m radius of her midden location (see figure S1 for a visual example of real spatial locations) and divided this count by the circle area, or `r round((pi*radius^2)/10000, 1)` hectares. The edges of trapping grids naturally had lower squirrel densities because grids were surrounded by habitat unsuitable for squirrels, such as marshes, aspen forests, or the Alaska highway. Therefore, we did not extrapolate squirrel densities outside of grid boundaries. Food supplementation caused an increase in local density over time.


Statistical Analysis

All data cleaning and statistical analyses were conducted using R language software (cite version). We standardized all numeric variables. Local density, tree cone density, cache size, and mother age were all standardized across all years and all grids. Litter size, litter growth rate, and Julian birth date were standardized within grid-year. Using the standardized cache size data, we categorized litters into three cache size levels: small (< 25% quantile), medium (> 25% and < 75% quantile), and large (> 75% quantile). Years were categorized as either mast years or regular years. We categorized litters into one of four treatment groups: controls, food adds with a bucket (henceforth, ‘bucket’), food add without a bucket (henceforth, ‘no bucket’), and rattle playbacks (henceforth, ‘rattle’).

To test how food availability and perceived density influence the relationship between litter size and growth rate in response to con-specific density, we used a multivariate Bayesian framework. To coherently meet the objectives of this study, we conducted three separate multivate Bayesian models using the ‘brms’ package (cite). Using the bf() function, we created two model formulas per analysis, one for each response variable, i.e., litter size and litter growth rate. We ran the models using the brm() function, merging both models into a bivariate analysis using the 'formula =' argument. We ran each model with `r core` cores and `r chain` chains, using `r warms` warm up and `r iters` iterations total. Analyses differed in what data was included and what categorical variable interacted with local density. However, all models included tree cone counts, mother age, mother age squared, parturition date, mast year, and litter sex ratio as fixed effects and grid-year and mother birth year as random effects.

The first analysis, called the 'Food Model', tested how food supplementation affected the relationship between litter size and growth rates in response to density. The Food Model used litters from control and food add grids across all years of the study (n = `r food[, .N]`). This data set therefore had three individual treatment groups: control, bucket, and no bucket. We interacted food treatment with density. No other fixed effects interacted.

The second analysis, called the 'Cache Model', tested how the mother's cache size affected the relationship between litter size and growth rates in response to density. The Cache Model used litters from control grids during years when midden cones were counted (n = `r cache[, .N]`). This data set therefore had three cache size categories: small, medium, and large. We interacted cache size with density. No other fixed effects interacted.

The third analysis, called the 'Rattle Model', tested how changes in perceived density, via rattle playbacks, affected the relationship between litter size and growth rates in response to density. The Rattle Model used litters from control and rattle grids during years when playback experiments occurred (n = `r rattle[, .N]`). This data set therefore had two treatments: rattles and controls. We interacted treatment with density. No other fixed effects interacted.
